title: The Ocean Has a False Bottom—and It Rises After Dark

# The Ocean Has a False Bottom—and It Rises After Dark
> **5 min · Oceans · Intermediate**

## The Hook

Imagine measuring the depth of the ocean and discovering that the bottom has moved upward overnight.

During World War II, sonar operators encountered something like this: an apparent seabed far shallower than expected, changing depth with the night. The instrument was receiving a real echo. Its interpretation was the problem.

That “bottom” was alive: a concentration of marine animals dense enough to return a conspicuous sound signal. Scientists call it the **deep scattering layer**. Its nightly movement turns a puzzling measurement into a glimpse of an enormous hidden migration. [NOAA explains the discovery](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/dsl/).

## The Short Answer

Many ocean animals spend daylight in deeper water, then swim upward after sunset to feed with less risk from predators that hunt by sight. Before daylight returns, they descend again. This daily commute is called **diel vertical migration**—“diel” simply means occurring over a 24-hour cycle—and NOAA describes it as the greatest migration on Earth. [NOAA’s migration overview](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/vertical-migration/).

The ocean’s surface may look peaceful while an immense crowd is changing floors underneath it.

## How It Works

**1. Sound reveals the crowd.**

Sonar sends a sound pulse into the water and listens for echoes. The time taken for an echo to return helps locate whatever reflected it. A strong return can come from the seafloor—or from animals suspended above it.

Gas-filled swim bladders in many fish are particularly effective sound reflectors. Enough animals together produce an acoustic layer: less a solid floor than a crowd visible to sound. NOAA reports that deep scattering layers are commonly detected around 300–500 metres down, though their depths vary. [NOAA’s explanation of scattering layers](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/dsl/).

**2. Darkness changes the risk of dinner.**

Feeding and hiding pull migrants in different directions. Shallower water offers food, but a visible animal risks becoming food itself.

Night gives it a better compromise. Darkness does not remove every predator, but it reduces the advantage of hunters that depend on light. Imagine a cafeteria with excellent snacks and terrible security: visiting after the lights dim can be worth a long journey.

**3. The commute has both a clock and outside cues.**

Their behaviour can follow an internal daily rhythm, adjusted by environmental cues. Light is especially important; temperature, prey and predation risk also matter. Avoiding visual predators is a leading explanation for many species, rather than a universal explanation for every animal. [NOAA’s overview of migration cues](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/vertical-migration/).

**4. Scientists can watch a journey unfold.**

On a 2021 expedition in the Gulf of Mexico, researchers recorded a scattering layer rising from roughly 500 metres to 100 metres, then descending again. That is about 400 metres each way in this particular observation—not a fixed itinerary for all oceans.

The team combined shipboard sound measurements with an underwater glider and drifting cameras. Sound followed the layer’s position; cameras supplied a closer look at its inhabitants. The pairing is useful because locating a crowd and understanding who is in it are different jobs. [NOAA’s expedition report](https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/expedition-feature/technology-development-partnerships-21scattering-layer-features-summary/).

## The Fascinating Part

This commute also carries **carbon**.

Near the surface, microscopic photosynthetic organisms incorporate carbon into living material. Animals eat that material, directly or through other animals. When migrants return to deeper water, the carbon in their meals travels with them. Feeding upstairs and returning downstairs therefore helps move carbon through the ocean.

There is another delivery route: sinking particles such as dead organisms and animal waste, collectively nicknamed **marine snow**. These processes contribute to the ocean’s **biological carbon pump**—the movement of carbon from surface waters toward depth.

The important qualification is that transport is not automatically permanent storage. Much sinking material becomes food along the way, and researchers still investigate how much carbon reaches deeper water and how long it stays there. The nightly migration is part of this system, not the whole pump. [Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution explains the carbon connection](https://www.whoi.edu/news-insights/content/the-ocean-twilight-zones-crucial-carbon-pump/).

A tiny animal’s dinner decision can therefore matter far beyond its own stomach. Multiply those journeys across the ocean and animal behaviour becomes part of how the planet moves carbon.

## 🧠 Think About This

If you could observe the ocean at only one time each day, how might your choice of hour change the world you thought existed beneath the surface?

## 🤯 One More Thing

Even the Arctic’s long winter darkness does not stop every light-linked migration. A 2016 study found widespread zooplankton movements associated with **moonlight**, including a rhythm of about 24.8 hours—the lunar day. The researchers suggested that avoiding predators able to hunt by moonlight could explain the behaviour. For these animals, “dark” has finer gradations than our eyes might suggest. [The original study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26774785/).
